title: Dark chocolate bars
question: How do you pick a dark chocolate bar?
decision: An occasional bar, short list, lower cocoa percentage.
why: Lab testing found more lead and cadmium as cocoa percentage climbed. Traditional guides keep chocolate occasional.
short_answer: Treat dark chocolate as a treat, not a daily habit. Higher cocoa percentages tested more likely to carry lead and cadmium, so a lower percentage is the steadier pick. Organic on the label did not mean lower metals in testing.
detail: Dark chocolate is generally at least 65 percent cacao. In independent lab testing, the higher the amount of cocoa, the more likely the lab found concerning levels of heavy metals like lead and cadmium. The same concern reaches hot cocoa and brownie and cake mixes. The testing advice: treat chocolate as a treat, try dark chocolates with lower cocoa percentages, do not assume organic dark chocolates are safer, do not give kids much dark chocolate, and think about total chocolate eaten across the week. Traditional guides list chocolate, cocoa and cacao among baking items to avoid and say chocolate should not be eaten habitually. A traditional chocolate maker in the same guide describes bars sweetened with whole cane sugar and no additives beyond nuts and spices.

title: Cornmeal, polenta and grits
question: How do you pick cornmeal, polenta or grits?
decision: Organic whole grain corn, lime-treated when offered, soaked first.
why: Traditional cooks soaked corn in lime water to soften it and release niacin. Guides avoid quick-cooking grains.
short_answer: Look for organic whole grain corn. Corn labeled nixtamalized, treated with lime, follows the traditional preparation. Soak cornmeal and polenta before cooking, and pass on quick-cooking grains.
detail: Native American cooks first soaked dry corn in lime water, a process called nixtamalization, which softens the corn and releases vitamin B3 that otherwise stays bound in the grain. Some then fermented the treated corn. Traditional shopping guides list organic whole grains as best, say all grains should be soaked in an acidic medium before cooking, and avoid non-organic grains and quick-cooking grains. A traditional grain guide says soaking in an acidic medium for seven hours is fine, and cooking in broth adds minerals. Hot cereals keep best bought in sealed packages rather than bins.

title: Wild rice
question: How do you pick wild rice?
decision: Wildcrafted wild rice, soaked seven hours before cooking.
why: Traditional guides name wildcrafted wild rice among the best grains and soak it before cooking.
short_answer: Look for wildcrafted wild rice, gathered from where it grows. Traditional guides list it with organic whole grains as the best choices. Soak it at least seven hours in warm water with a splash of something sour before cooking.
detail: Wild rice was a traditional food of the Great Lakes peoples. Traditional shopping guides list wildcrafted wild rice among the best grains, alongside organic whole grain rice and dried beans, and say all grains should be soaked in an acidic medium. A traditional recipe soaks wild rice in warm water with whey, yogurt, kefir, buttermilk, lemon juice or vinegar for at least seven hours, then simmers it with broth. Grains keep best bought in sealed packages rather than bins.

title: Salad dressing

short_answer: Look for a dressing built on olive oil with a short list. The more ingredients, the more likely a bottle carries additives like EDTA, artificial colors or propylene glycol. Traditional guides pass on soybean, canola and vegetable oils.
detail: An ingredient review of salad dressings found that the more ingredients, the more likely a bottle contained problem ingredients.
